161.event_title: Robert Schumann hails the young Chopin and the young Brahms
161.event: In 1831 the young Robert Schumann, himself an aspiring composer, published his first piece of music criticism in the Leipzig Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung, a review that greeted the unknown Frederic Chopin as a genius. In 1853, after the twenty-year-old Johannes Brahms visited the Schumanns in Dusseldorf and played them his unpublished works, Schumann wrote the article New Paths in the Neue Zeitschrift fur Musik, presenting Brahms to the musical world. Yale University Library notes that his two best-remembered reviews, the first and last of his critical career, each hailed the arrival of a young genius.
161.explanation: Schumann, a leading composer and the most influential music critic of his day, repeatedly used his position to lift up younger rivals rather than guard his own standing.
161.tie_back: The kural asks that a heart free of envy be made the settled rule of one's conduct, and Schumann's whole critical career, from first article to last, was built on celebrating others' gifts.
161._accuracy_note: A strong pattern of generous, envy-free conduct across a career, though the sources record his praise rather than any explicit inner freedom from envy.

162.event_title: Nishida and Oe make the Medals of Friendship
162.event: At the Berlin Olympic Games, the Japanese pole vaulters Shuhei Nishida and Sueo Oe both cleared 4.25 metres and tied for second place after a final lasting more than five hours. The placings were settled by the Japanese side, with the older Nishida given the silver medal and Oe the bronze. After returning to Japan, the two friends had both medals cut in half and joined, so that each man kept a medal that was half silver and half bronze, which became known in Japan as the Medals of Friendship.
162.explanation: Rather than let a ranking divide them, two rivals in the same event chose to share the honour equally, and Nishida's medal is now displayed by Waseda University.
162.tie_back: The kural says no gain equals freedom from envy toward anyone at all, and Nishida and Oe valued their friendship above the difference between silver and bronze.
162._accuracy_note: A vivid case of two direct rivals refusing to let comparison of rank breed envy, though it concerns one episode rather than freedom from envy toward everyone.

163.event_title: Haydn praises Mozart to his father
163.event: In February 1785 Joseph Haydn, then the most celebrated composer in Europe, heard the last three of Mozart's new string quartets played at a gathering in Vienna where Mozart's father Leopold was present. Haydn told Leopold that his son was the greatest composer he knew either in person or by reputation, and that he had taste and the deepest knowledge of composition; Leopold reported the remark in a letter to his daughter. Mozart dedicated the six quartets to Haydn when they were published later that year, calling him his dear friend.
163.explanation: Haydn, the established master, openly rejoiced in the rise of a younger composer who could have been seen as his rival, and their mutual admiration enriched both men's music.
163.tie_back: The kural condemns envying another's prosperity instead of welcoming it, and Haydn did the opposite, welcoming Mozart's genius with generous praise.
163._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the positive side of the kural: an established master actively welcoming a rival's success.

164.event_title: Darwin refuses to act in a paltry spirit toward Wallace
164.place: Down House, Kent, and the Linnean Society, London, England
164.event: In June 1858 Charles Darwin, who had worked on natural selection for about twenty years without publishing, received an essay from Alfred Russel Wallace setting out the same theory. Writing to Charles Lyell on 25 June, Darwin asked whether he could honourably publish his own sketch now and said he would rather burn his whole book than have Wallace or anyone think he had behaved meanly. Lyell and Joseph Hooker arranged for Wallace's essay and extracts from Darwin's earlier writings to be read together at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858.
164.explanation: Darwin faced the loss of credit for his life's work, yet he refused to suppress or outrun his rival, and the joint reading gave both men their place.
164.tie_back: The kural says the wise, knowing where wrongdoing leads, will not do wrong out of envy, and Darwin refused to act unfairly toward a rival even when his priority was at stake.
164._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of declining to act from rivalry; the joint presentation itself was arranged by Lyell and Hooker, not by Darwin alone.

165.event_title: The Bone Wars ruin Cope and Marsh
165.place: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; New Haven, Connecticut; and the American West, United States
165.event: The palaeontologists Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh, once friends, spent decades in a bitter competition to find and name dinosaur fossils in the American West. In January 1890 Cope gave a journalist material accusing Marsh of plagiarism and misuse of federal funds, and the New York Herald ran the charges for weeks. Congress then cut the Geological Survey's budget, Marsh lost his paleontology post and had to hand over many fossils, while Cope, who had already lost his fortune, was left with little but his collection and died in 1897.
165.explanation: PBS and National Geographic describe the feud as ruining both men, who did each other far more damage than any outside opponent.
165.tie_back: The kural says envy alone is enough to destroy the envious even if no enemy harms them, and Cope and Marsh's rivalry brought down both of them.
165._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of self-destroying rivalry, though the sources speak of rivalry and feud rather than naming envy as such.

166.event_title: Benedict Arnold resents promotions given to others
166.place: Philadelphia, West Point (New York) and London
166.event: In February 1777 the Continental Congress promoted five brigadier generals junior to Benedict Arnold to major general and passed him over, and Arnold felt his honour insulted and threatened to resign. Although he was later made a major general, his seniority was not restored, and Mount Vernon and History.com describe his resentment over promotion as a motive for his later treason. In 1780 his plot to hand West Point to the British was discovered; he fled to the British side and spent his last years in England, distrusted on both sides of the Atlantic, dying in London in 1801.
166.explanation: A brave and gifted commander allowed grievance over honours granted to others to turn into betrayal, and lost both his reputation and his country.
166.tie_back: The kural warns that one who resents what is given to others will perish together with his household, and Arnold's resentment of others' promotions led to his disgrace and exile.
166._accuracy_note: Resentment of honours given to others is well documented as one motive, but his ruin was not literal want of food and clothing, and debt also played a part.

167.event_title: Li Si brings down his gifted schoolmate Han Fei
167.event: Han Fei, a brilliant Legalist thinker whose writings the King of Qin admired, came to the Qin court on a diplomatic mission in 233 BCE. According to Britannica, Li Si, the chief minister and Han Fei's former schoolmate, apparently fearing that Han Fei might win the king's favour with his superior learning, had him imprisoned, and Han Fei died in prison. Li Si rose to great power under the First Emperor, but after the emperor's death he fell out with the eunuch Zhao Gao, who had him executed in 208 BCE.
167.explanation: Li Si removed a more gifted rival and reached the summit of power, yet his fortune did not last and he ended in ruin.
167.tie_back: The kural pictures fortune deserting the envious and handing him over to misfortune, and Li Si's high fortune ended in disgrace and death.
167._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Li Si's rivalry with Han Fei is documented, but his own downfall came from a later power struggle, not directly from that envy.

168.event_title: The Pazzi conspiracy against the Medici
168.event: Members of the Pazzi family, a rival Florentine banking house, joined a plot to overthrow the ruling Medici, and on 26 April 1478 conspirators attacked Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici during Mass in Florence Cathedral, killing Giuliano and wounding Lorenzo. The people of Florence rallied to the Medici, the plot collapsed, and the conspirators were pursued and punished. The Pazzi family was stripped of its riches and banished, while Lorenzo emerged with his power strengthened.
168.explanation: Instead of competing fairly, the Pazzi tried to seize a rival's position by crime, and the attempt destroyed their own wealth and standing.
168.tie_back: The kural says envy destroys a man's wealth and drives him onto the path of evil, and the Pazzi lost their fortune after turning to a criminal plot against their rivals.
168._accuracy_note: Rivalry leading to crime and loss of wealth fits well, but the sources call the Pazzi rivals and do not explicitly name envy as their motive.

169.event_title: Aristides the Just is ostracised and then recalled
169.event: Aristides, an Athenian statesman renowned for his honesty and known as the Just, was ostracised in 482 BCE after political manoeuvring by his rival Themistocles and accusations of sympathy with Persia. When Xerxes invaded, the Athenians recalled the ostracised exiles in 480 BCE, and Aristides led a hoplite force at the battle of Salamis. In 479 BCE he was one of the Athenian commanders at the victory of Plataea.
169.explanation: An upright man suffered exile while his rival prevailed, yet within two years his city recalled him and gave him high command.
169.tie_back: The kural invites reflection on the puzzle of the upright suffering misfortune, and Aristides' exile, soon reversed, shows such misfortune need not last.
169._accuracy_note: A clear case of an upright man's undeserved misfortune that later reversed, though it does not show an envious man prospering for long.

170.event_title: Alfred Russel Wallace, Darwin's greatest champion, is showered with honours
170.event: After the joint reading of 1858, Charles Darwin's name came to dominate the theory of natural selection that Alfred Russel Wallace had reached independently. The Natural History Museum notes that Wallace expressed no resentment and was Darwin's greatest supporter, and in 1889 he titled his own book on the theory Darwinism. Wallace rose to the highest ranks of science, receiving the Royal Society's Darwin Medal in 1890 and, in 1908, both its Copley Medal and the Order of Merit.
170.explanation: Wallace's lack of resentment did not cost him: he was honoured throughout his long life as a leading naturalist.
170.tie_back: The kural says no one free from envy has ever fallen from prosperity, and Wallace, who never begrudged Darwin his fame, received the highest honours of his day.
170._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of an envy-free life that flourished, though the kural's universal claim cannot be proved by a single life.
